newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China exports recovering but seen flat this year.
newsitem.headline: China exports recovering but seen flat this year.

text.p: China is already recovering from a sudden slide in exports earlier this year but economists said on Monday that the world's largest developing nation would be lucky to attain zero export growth for the entire year.

"Year-to-year it's still negative, but exports grew by 12 percent in August, which is the highest this year. For the year, I think it'll probably be at about zero," said Kevin Chan, economist with Salomon Brothers in Hong Kong.

Along with other exporting nations in Asia, China suffered from weak U.S. consumer markets in the first half with particular weakness in its exports to Hong Kong and Taiwan, much of which are then re-exported to the United States.

A very high base of comparison highlighted China's poor performance. This year's forecast of zero growth contrasts sharply with a 22.9-percent rise in exports from China last year, including a sudden first quarter spurt of 80 percent.
China has been relatively quick to recover from the downturn, but economists warn longer-term trends are afoot that are slowly changing the face of China as an exporting nation.

Foreign funded enterprises (FFEs) are catching up with, and could soon overtake, state owned enterprises (SOEs) as the primary drivers of China's export engine, and this could have implications for public policy.

"China's domestic exporters have been lobbying for a devaluation of the Renminbi, arguing that this will help to reduce losses and correct the trade deficit," economist Heidi Hong said in a recent ING Barings report.
"(But) government assistance is not justified on the grounds that SOEs are commanding a smaller share of total exports."
SOEs' contribution to total exports fell to 56.9 percent in the first five months this year compared with 71.1 percent in the same period last year, ING Barings said.
By comparison, FFEs' share of total exports rose to 40.9 percent against 27.4 percent last year.
Even more striking, economists in Hong Kong have all noticed a foreign investment shift away from southern China in favour of cheaper parts of Southeast Asia such as Vietnam.

Economists said there are numerous reasons for the shift. Southern China's geographical location increases its vulnerability to cyclical downturns in overseas markets and regional political factors, such as strained China-Taiwan relations and unresolved Sino-U.S. trade disputes.

"(It is also) a result of the expansion of outward processing activities in southern China plateauing after more than a decade of massive relocation of production bases from Hong Kong and Taiwan into this area," said Hong.
While economists all agree the shift is occurring, interpretations of its significance vary.
Ken Chan, senior economist at Nikko Securities, said lower value-added investment is slowly moving away from southern China, but higher value added investment is increasing.
"Southern China will have a more difficult time but I don't think it will lose its edge. It will remain an important trading area for China," Chan said.

Kevin Chan at Salomon agreed that southern China's labour costs are high compared to other parts of Indochina, including central China, but they are also relatively cheap compared to other Asian nations such as Singapore, and even Thailand.

"And when you talk about labour costs, you have to look at quality as well," Kevin Chan said. "The quality may not match the costs, especially for the United States, which has strict quality control requirements, and especially in electronics."
